A particle moves with a constant acceleration of (3i−2j)m/s2. The velocity of the particle is 2im/s when t=0s. Find the time when the velocity of the particle equals (14i−8j)m/s.

EXPLANATION

Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time t can be found using

v=u+at,

where u is the initial velocity, and a is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting

a=3i−2j,u=2i,v=14i−8j

into the equation above, we can solve for t, as follows:

v=u+at14i−8j=2i+(3i−2j)t12i−8j=(3i−2j)t12i−8j=3ti−2tj

Equating the i and j components in the last equation, we obtain {12=3t−8=−2t⟹t=4s.

after.problem: A particle moves with a constant acceleration of $(3i-2j)\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$ The velocity of the particle is $2i\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}.$ Find the time when the velocity of the particle equals $(14i-8j)\,\text{m/s}.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting 

$$
a=3i-2j,\,u=2i,\,v=14i-8j
$$

into the equation above, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\ 14i-8j & =2i+(3i-2j)t \\ 12i-8j & =(3i-2j)t \\ 12i-8j & =3ti-2tj\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the $i$ and $j$ components in the last equation, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}12 & = & 3t \\ -8 & = & -2t\end{aligned}\,⟹\,t=4\,\text{s}.
$$

after.problem: Given that ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are the solutions of the equation $2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1=0$ for $-\pi <x\le \pi ,$ what is the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating $\operatorname{sin}⁡x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡x+1 & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the principal value:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{\pi }{6}$ lies inside the required domain, our first solution is ${x}_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Our first solution lies in the fourth quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$

![](@asset-0@)

A second solution $X$ lies in the $3$rd quadrant, and we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}X & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

However, this value is not in the required domain. To get the second solution ${x}_{2}$ that's within the given domain, we simply subtract $2\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}=X-2\pi  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}-2\pi =-\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-\frac{5\pi }{6},-\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=(-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot (-\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{36}.
$$

after.problem:
Evaluate the integral
${\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x.
$$

So, let $u=1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $\pi /2$ | $3\pi /4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $1+\sqrt{2}$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{u}\,(-\text{d}u) \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|{|}_{2}^{1+\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+\sqrt{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{2}{1+\sqrt{2}}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2\sqrt{2}-2)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3},\, & 0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find $P(Y<X<Y+2).$
after.worked_solution:
If $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability density function for the random variables $X$ and $Y$ and $A⊂{R}^{2},$ then

$$
P((X,Y)\in A)={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y.
$$

Notice that $f(x,y)$ is nonnegative in the region $D=[0,3]\times [0,1],$ and the event $A={Y<X<Y+2}$ corresponds to a subset of $D,$ shown as the shaded region below:

![](assets/f4a0cc357eee835c84ef08524d27e3c30b98d58e1b6b5083b7df6a66ce987b6b.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y<X<Y+2) & ={∬}_{A}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{A}\frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\text{Area}(A) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
We split the integral into the sum of two integrals and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{3}{1+{t}^{2}}+{t}^{2})\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3(\operatorname{arctan}⁡1-\operatorname{arctan}⁡0)+\frac{1}{3}({1}^{3}-{0}^{1}) \\  & =3(\frac{\pi }{4}-0)+\frac{1}{3}(1-0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{9\pi +4}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find dim(Null(E)), we reduce E to row echelon form, as follows:

E=[1−23112−4622001−2300−12−3]R2:=R2+(−2)R1∼[1−231100000001−2300−12−3]R4:=R4+R3∼[1−231100000001−2300000].

The reduced matrix has 2 pivot columns and 3 non-pivot columns (namely, the 2nd, 4th, and 5th columns).

dim(Null(E))=3.

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=2cos⁡t,y=sin2⁡t,t∈[0,π]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
4π∫0πcos⁡t1+3sin2⁡tdt
b
25π∫0πsin4⁡tdt
c
4π∫0πsin⁡tdt
d
2π∫0πsin2⁡t4+cos⁡tdt
e
4π∫0πsin3⁡t1+cos2⁡tdt
Don't Know
Submit

Question 8

Consider the curve defined parametrically as x=2cos⁡t,y=sin2⁡t,t∈[0,π]. What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
4π∫0πcos⁡t1+3sin2⁡tdt
b
25π∫0πsin4⁡tdt
c
4π∫0πsin⁡tdt
d
2π∫0πsin2⁡t4+cos⁡tdt
e
4π∫0πsin3⁡t1+cos2⁡tdt
Don't Know
Submit
Skipped Question
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

ds=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt.

We are told that the limits of integration are from t1=0 to t2=π.

Computing the derivatives, we get

dxdt=ddt(2cos⁡t)=−2sin⁡tdydt=ddt(sin2⁡t)=2sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore,

S=2π∫t1t2y(dxdt)2+(dydt)2dt=2π∫0πsin2⁡t(−2sin⁡t)2+(2sin⁡tcos⁡t)2dt=2π∫0πsin2⁡t4sin2⁡t+4sin2⁡tcos2⁡tdt=2π∫0πsin2⁡t4sin2⁡t(1+cos2⁡t)dt=2π∫0πsin2⁡t⋅|2sin⁡t|1+cos2⁡tdt=4π∫0πsin3⁡t1+cos2⁡tdt.

after.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,t\in [0,\pi ].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}⁡t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t(1+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot |2\operatorname{sin}⁡t|\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{3}⁡t\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Given that the function f(x)=x4+2x2−x has a critical point in the interval [0,1], use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from x0=0.5 to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places.

a
x≈0.27
b
x≈0.24
c
x≈0.29
d
x≈0.20
e
x≈0.21
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

xn+1=xn−f′(xn)f″(xn),

where f′(xn) and f″(xn) are the first and second derivatives of f(x) evaluated at xn, respectively.

In our case, we have

f′(x)=(x4+2x2−x)′=4x3+4x−1,f″(x)=(4x3+4x−1)′=12x2+4.

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

xn+1=xn−4xn3+4xn−112xn2+4=xn(12xn2+4)−(4xn3+4xn−1)12xn2+4=8xn3+112xn2+4.

Starting with x0=0.5, we have

x1=8x03+112x02+4=8(0.5)3+112(0.5)2+4=0.285714….

Similarly, we have

x2=8x13+112x12+4=8(0.285714…)3+112(0.285714…)2+4=0.238290…,x3=8x23+112x22+4=8(0.238290…)3+112(0.238290…)2+4=0.236734….

Notice that the last two approximations x2≈0.24 and x3≈0.24 are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is x≈0.24, rounded to two decimal places.

after.problem: Given that the function $f(x)={x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}-x$ has a critical point in the interval $[0,1],$ use the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting from ${x}_{0}=0.5$ to estimate the critical point. Round your final answer to two decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}-x)^{′}=4{x}^{3}+4x-1, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(4{x}^{3}+4x-1)^{′}=12{x}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{4{x}_{n}^{3}+4{x}_{n}-1}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(12{x}_{n}^{2}+4)-(4{x}_{n}^{3}+4{x}_{n}-1)}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8{x}_{n}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{n}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{8{x}_{0}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{0}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.5)^{3}+1}{12(0.5)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.285\,714….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{8{x}_{1}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{1}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.285\,714…)^{3}+1}{12(0.285\,714…)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.238\,290…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{8{x}_{2}^{3}+1}{12{x}_{2}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{8(0.238\,290…)^{3}+1}{12(0.238\,290…)^{2}+4} \\  & =0.236\,734….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.24$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.24$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.24,$ rounded to two decimal places.

EXPLANATION

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

xn+1=xn−f′(xn)f″(xn),

where f′(xn) and f″(xn) are the first and second derivatives of f(x) evaluated at xn, respectively.

In our case, we have

f′(x)=(x2+e−x)′=2x−e−x,f″(x)=(2x−e−x)′=2+e−x.

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

xn+1=xn−2xn−e−xn2+e−xn=xn(2+e−xn)−(2xn−e−xn)2+e−xn=(xn+1)e−xn2+e−xn.

Starting with x0=1.0, we have

x1=(x0+1)e−x02+e−x0=(1.0+1)e−1.02+e−1.0=0.310725….

Similarly, we have

x2=(x1+1)e−x12+e−x1=(0.310725…+1)e−0.310725…2+e−0.310725…=0.351511…,x3=(x2+1)e−x22+e−x2=(0.351511…+1)e−0.351511…2+e−0.351511…=0.351733….

Notice that the last two approximations x2≈0.35 and x3≈0.35 are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is x≈0.35, rounded to two decimal places.

after.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}+{e}^{-x})^{′}=2x-{e}^{-x}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(2x-{e}^{-x})^{′}=2+{e}^{-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{2{x}_{n}-{e}^{-{x}_{n}}}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{n}}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(2+{e}^{-{x}_{n}})-(2{x}_{n}-{e}^{-{x}_{n}})}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{n}}} \\  & =\frac{({x}_{n}+1){e}^{-{x}_{n}}}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{n}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=1.0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{({x}_{0}+1){e}^{-{x}_{0}}}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{0}}} \\  & =\frac{(1.0+1){e}^{-1.0}}{2+{e}^{-1.0}} \\  & =0.310\,725….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{({x}_{1}+1){e}^{-{x}_{1}}}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{1}}} \\  & =\frac{(0.310\,725…+1){e}^{-0.310\,725…}}{2+{e}^{-0.310\,725…}} \\  & =0.351\,511…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{({x}_{2}+1){e}^{-{x}_{2}}}{2+{e}^{-{x}_{2}}} \\  & =\frac{(0.351\,511…+1){e}^{-0.351\,511…}}{2+{e}^{-0.351\,511…}} \\  & =0.351\,733….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.35$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.35$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.35,$ rounded to two decimal places.

before.html:
Question 11
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=3sin⁡(3t), where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=5 and velocity v=1 when t=0, calculate the position x of the particle at time t.

a
x(t)=t+13sin⁡(3t)+5
b
x(t)=2t−3cos⁡(3t)+8
c
x(t)=2t−13sin⁡(3t)+5
d
x(t)=cos⁡(3t)+4
e
x(t)=2t+3sin⁡(3t)+5
Don't Know
Submit

Question 11
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=3sin⁡(3t), where t≥0 is the time. If the particle has position x=5 and velocity v=1 when t=0, calculate the position x of the particle at time t.

a
x(t)=t+13sin⁡(3t)+5
b
x(t)=2t−3cos⁡(3t)+8
c
x(t)=2t−13sin⁡(3t)+5
d
x(t)=cos⁡(3t)+4
e
x(t)=2t+3sin⁡(3t)+5
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫3sin⁡(3t)dt=−cos⁡(3t)+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(0)=1. Substituting this into the above gives

1=−cos⁡(3(0))+C1=−1+CC=2.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=2−cos⁡(3t).

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(2−cos⁡(3t))dt=2t−13sin⁡(3t)+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(0)=5. Substituting this into the above gives

5=2(0)−13sin⁡(3(0))+KK=5.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=2t−13sin⁡(3t)+5.

after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=5$ and velocity $v=1$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(0))+C \\ 1 & =-1+C \\ C & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\text{d}t \\  & =2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=5.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =2(0)-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3(0))+K \\ K & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=2t-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+5.
$$

Question 12
?

A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin O with acceleration a(t)=1t2, where t≥1 is the time. If the particle has position x=4 and velocity v=0 when t=1, calculate the position x of the particle at time t≥1.

a
x(t)=−ln⁡t+2t
b
 x(t)=ln⁡t−2t+4
c
x(t)=ln⁡t+2
d
x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+3
e
 x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+1
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity v(t):

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫1t2dt=−1t+C

To determine C, we use the fact that v(1)=0. Substituting this into the above gives

0=−11+CC=1.

So the velocity is given by v(t)=−1t+1.

Now, we integrate the velocity to get x(t):

x(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫(−1t+1)dt=−ln⁡t+t+K

To determine K, we use the fact that x(1)=4. Substituting this into the above gives

4=−ln⁡(1)+1+K4=−0+1+KK=3.

Therefore, the position x of the particle at time t is x(t)=−ln⁡t+t+3.
after.name: Question 12
after.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},$ where $t\ge 1$ is the time. If the particle has position $x=4$ and velocity $v=0$ when $t=1,$ calculate the position $x$ of the particle at time $t\ge 1.$
after.worked_solution:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{1}{1}+C \\ C & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=-\frac{1}{t}+1.$

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{1}{t}+1)\text{d}t \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K,$ we use the fact that $x(1)=4.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+K \\ 4 & =-0+1+K \\ K & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)=-\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t+3.
$$

Let's start by writing the matrix S−λI: ﻿﻿﻿S−λI=[−8−λ4−54−λ].

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation det(S−λI)=0: det(S−λI)=0|−8−λ4−54−λ|=0(−8−λ)(4−λ)−4⋅(−5)=0−32+8λ−4λ+λ2+20=0λ2+4λ−12=0

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find all real eigenvalues of the matrix
$S=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 4 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
Let's start by writing the matrix $S-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
S-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}].
$$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(S-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(S-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-8-\lambda  & 4 \\ -5 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-8-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4\cdot (-5) & =0 \\ -32+8\lambda -4\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}+4\cdot 1\cdot 12}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{64}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm 8}{2} \\  & =-6,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-6$ and $\lambda =2.$

Now, let's find and solve the characteristic equation $det(R-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(R-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 2 \\ -5 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(6-\lambda )-2\cdot (-5) & =0 \\ -30+5\lambda -6\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}+10 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -20 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{(-1)^{2}+4\cdot 1\cdot 20}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1\pm \sqrt{81}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1\pm 9}{2} \\  & =-4,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are $\lambda =-4$ and $\lambda =5.$

Newton’s second law states that F=ma, where F is the resultant force, m is the mass, and a is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate r to get the velocity vector:

v=drdt=⟨ddt(t3),ddt(t4−t2)⟩=⟨3t2,4t3−2t⟩

a=dvdt=⟨ddt(3t2),ddt(4t3−2t)⟩=⟨6t,12t2−2⟩

Therefore, the resultant force F at time t equals

F=ma=3⋅⟨6t,12t2−2⟩=⟨18t,36t2−6⟩.

When t=4s, we have

F(4)=⟨18(4),36(42)−6⟩=⟨72,570⟩.

after.worked_solution:
Newton’s second law states that

$$
F=ma,
$$

 
where $F$ is the *resultant* force, $m$ is the mass, and $a$ is the acceleration.

To compute the acceleration vector, we first differentiate $r$ to get the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate the velocity vector to get the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resultant force $F$ at time $t$ equals

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =ma \\  & =3\cdot ⟨6t,\,12{t}^{2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨18t,\,36{t}^{2}-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

When $t=4\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(4) & =⟨18(4),\,36({4}^{2})-6⟩ \\  & =⟨72,\,570⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the magnitude of $F(4)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}|F(4)| & =\sqrt{(72)^{2}+{(570)}^{2}} \\  & ≈575\,\text{N}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest Newton.

EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

We are told that the limits of integration are from y1=1 to y2=e.

Computing the derivative, we get

dxdy=ddy(y312+1y)=y4−44y2⇒(dxdy)2=y8−8y4+1616y4.

Therefore,

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy=2π∫1ey1+y8−8y4+1616y4dy=2π∫1eyy8+8y4+1616y4dy=2π∫1ey(y4+4)216y4dy=2π∫1ey(y4+44y2)dy=π2∫1ey4+4ydy=π2∫1e(y3+4y)dy=π2(y44+4ln⁡y)|1e=π2(e44+4−14)=π8(e4+15).
after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\frac{{y}^{3}}{12}+\frac{1}{y}$ that lies between the lines $y=1$ and $y=e.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=1$ to ${y}_{2}=e.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{12}+\frac{1}{y})=\frac{{y}^{4}-4}{4{y}^{2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}=\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{\frac{{y}^{8}+8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\,y\sqrt{\frac{({y}^{4}+4)^{2}}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y(\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{4{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}({y}^{3}+\frac{4}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{{e}^{4}}{4}+4-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}({e}^{4}+15).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{1+\frac{{y}^{8}-8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y\sqrt{\frac{{y}^{8}+8{y}^{4}+16}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\,y\sqrt{\frac{({y}^{4}+4)^{2}}{16{y}^{4}}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}y(\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{4{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{{y}^{4}+4}{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}({y}^{3}+\frac{4}{y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{(\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(\frac{{e}^{4}}{4}+4-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}({e}^{4}+15).\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={y}^{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡x-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$
after.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants:

Additionally, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡x-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}) \\  & ={y}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & ={y}^{3}\cdot (-{csc}^{2}⁡x)-{y}^{2}\cdot (2x) \\  & =-{y}^{3}{csc}^{2}⁡x-2x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =-(1)^{3}\cdot {csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2}\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =-1\cdot 1-\pi  \\  & =-1-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Question 19

Find the interval where the function f(t)=u(t)g(t) is differentiable, given that u(t)=2−tg(t)=t2i+etj+ln⁡(1−t)k

a
 (−∞,2)
b
 (−∞,1)
c
 (1,2)
d
 (−∞,0]
e
 (−∞,1)∪(2,∞)
Don't Know
Submit
Skipped Question
EXPLANATION

The function f(t)=u(t)g(t) is differentiable on the common domain where both u(t) and g(t) are differentiable. The vector function g(t) is differentiable on the common domain where its components are differentiable.

Let's now find the intervals where each of the functions u(t) and g(t) are differentiable.

For the real-valued function u(t), note that it is differentiable over (−∞,2).

For the function g(t):

  • The first component, t2, is differentiable for all values of t.

  • The second component, et, is differentiable for all values of t.

  • The third component, ln⁡(1−t), is differentiable on (−∞,1).

Therefore, the intersection of the domains of all three components of g(t) is (−∞,1).

Finally, the common domain of differentiability for u(t) and g(t) is (−∞,1)∩(−∞,2)=(−∞,1).

A={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,1<{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4}.

after.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

In this case, the set $A$ and its boundary $∂A={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ are shown below.

![](assets/a39ecae41a88e873fa9eecb30a5b554be9ec98cf630851715ab35f2f873710f2.png)

   

The interior of a set $A,$ denoted $\text{int}\,A,$ is the set containing all the interior points of $A.$ It contains every point in $A$ except the boundary points: 

$$
\text{int}\,A=A-∂A
$$

The interior of $A$ is shown below.

![](assets/5e473584ef5193b434ff6c138b08c4fbd9111a37252019143b1afb2d48c913c6.png)

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statements I and III are false. Since ${C}_{1}⊂∂A-A,$ we must have that $∂A⊄A$ and also that $A\ne ∂A\cup \text{int}A.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{int}\,A$ contains all points in $A$ except the boundary points, we must have $A-∂A=\text{int}\,A.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

after.name: Question 21
after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+8$ is strictly increasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}-3\cdot 2x \\  & =6{x}^{2}-6x,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-6x & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
6x(x-1)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=6x(x-1)$ has roots at $x=0$ and $x=1,$ as shown below:

![](assets/ec7ea6baa82d60a6cf472c904460190042d889d86cb092b19d9809111bd93b36.png)

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals $x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (1,\infty ).$

Question 22
?

Find the values of x for which the function f(x)=(x2−8)ex is strictly increasing.

a
x<−2 and x>4
b
−2<x<4
c
−4<x<2
d
−2<x<2
e
x<−4 and x>2
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The function is strictly increasing where f′(x)>0. Differentiating f(x) using the product rule, we get

f′(x)=(x2−8)ex+2xex=(x2+2x−8)ex,

so we need to solve the inequality (x2+2x−8)ex>0.

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to x2+2x−8>0.

The above inequality factors as (x−2)(x+4)>0.

The graph of y=(x−2)(x+4) has roots at x=2 and x=−4, as shown below:

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals x<−4 and x>2.
after.name: Question 22
after.problem: Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=({x}^{2}-8){e}^{x}$ is strictly increasing.
after.worked_solution:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x)$ using the product rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=({x}^{2}-8){e}^{x}+2x{e}^{x}=({x}^{2}+2x-8){e}^{x},\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
({x}^{2}+2x-8){e}^{x}>0.
$$

The exponential function is always positive, so this reduces to

$$
{x}^{2}+2x-8>0.
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
(x-2)(x+4)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=(x-2)(x+4)$ has roots at $x=2$ and $x=-4,$ as shown below:

![](assets/d3f7d0a5a5bf14b567a57b780a94509e3f039c6bd853ec6e3cadcf2e20790dea.png)

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals $x<-4$ and $x>2.$

Question 23
?

Calculate d2ydx2 for the polar curve r=csc⁡θ.

a
−csc⁡θ
b
12csc2⁡θ
c
sin2⁡θ
d
0
e
csc2⁡θ
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

d2ydx2=ddθ(dydx)(dxdθ).

First, we need to find dydx and dxdθ.

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of θ.

Using the fact that r=csc⁡θ, we get

x=cot⁡θ,y=1.

Then, to find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

x′(θ)=−csc2⁡θ,y′(θ)=0.

Therefore,

dydx=0−csc2⁡θ=0.

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

d2ydx2=ddθ(0)−csc2⁡θ=0−csc2⁡θ=0.

after.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 24
?

Calculate d2ydx2 for the polar curve r=3.

a
−13csc3⁡θ
b
 −3csc3⁡θ
c
 13csc⁡θ
d
 3csc3⁡θ
e
 13csc2⁡θ
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

d2ydx2=ddθ(dydx)(dxdθ).

First, we need to find dydx and dxdθ.

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of θ.

Using the fact that r=3, we get

x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ.

Then, to find dydx we use the rule

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ).

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

x′(θ)=−3sin⁡θ,y′(θ)=3cos⁡θ.

Therefore,

dydx=3cos⁡θ−3sin⁡θ=−cot⁡θ.

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

d2ydx2=ddθ(−cot⁡θ)−3sin⁡θ=csc2⁡θ−3sin⁡θ=−13csc3⁡θ.
after.name: Question 24
after.problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=3.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=3,$ we get

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{csc}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

before.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=t{e}^{-t},\,t\ge 0.

Question 25
?

A particle P is traveling along the x-axis with displacement s(t) from a fixed origin O given by s(t)=te−t,t≥0. Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

a
t=2,v=1e2
b
t=3,v=3e3
c
t=1,v=1e
d
t=2,v=−1e2
e
t=3,v=−1e3
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate v(t) by differentiating s(t):

v(t)=dsdt=ddt(te−t)=(1−t)e−t

Now, we differentiate v(t) to find a(t): a(t)=dvdt=ddt((1−t)e−t)=(t−2)e−t

Next, we put a=0 to find the time when the acceleration is zero: 0=(t−2)e−tt−2=0t=2

So the acceleration is zero when t=2. To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into v(t) to get v(2)=(1−(2))e−(2)=−e−2=−1e2.
after.name: Question 25
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=t{e}^{-t},\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t{e}^{-t}) \\  & =(1-t){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}((1-t){e}^{-t}) \\  & =(t-2){e}^{-t}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(t-2){e}^{-t} \\ t-2 & =0 \\ t & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t=2.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =(1-(2)){e}^{-(2)} \\  & =-{e}^{-2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{e}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 26
?

A particle P is traveling along the x-axis with displacement s(t) from a fixed origin O given by s(t)=t2ln⁡(t),t≥0. Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

a
t=e−3/2,v=−2e−3/2
b
t=e−1/2,v=−2e−1/2
c
t=e−5/2,v=−e−3/2
d
t=e−5/2,v=−2e−5/2
e
t=e−3/2,v=−e−3/2
Don't Know
Submit

before.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

a
t=e−3/2,v=−2e−3/2
b
t=e−1/2,v=−2e−1/2
c
t=e−5/2,v=−e−3/2
d
t=e−5/2,v=−2e−5/2
e
t=e−3/2,v=−e−3/2
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we calculate v(t) by differentiating s(t):

v(t)=dsdt=ddt(t2ln⁡(t))=2tln⁡(t)+t

Now, we differentiate v(t) to find a(t): a(t)=dvdt=ddt(t+2tln⁡(t))=2ln⁡(t)+3

Next, we put a=0 to find the time when the acceleration is zero: 0=2ln⁡(t)+32ln⁡(t)=−3ln⁡(t)=−32t=e−3/2

So the acceleration is zero when t=e−3/2. To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into v(t) to get v(e−3/2)=2(e−3/2)ln⁡(e−3/2)+e−3/2=2e−3/2(−32)+e−3/2=−2e−3/2.
after.name: Question 26
after.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)={t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t),\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.
after.worked_solution:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+t\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2t\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t)+3 \\ 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-3 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(t) & =-\frac{3}{2} \\ t & ={e}^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

So the acceleration is zero when $t={e}^{-3/2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v({e}^{-3/2}) & =2({e}^{-3/2})\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-3/2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =2{e}^{-3/2}(-\frac{3}{2})+{e}^{-3/2} \\  & =-2{e}^{-3/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Recall that for any affine transformation T:u⟶Au+b, where A is a 2×2 matrix and u and b are 2×1 column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

  • If T is non-singular, i.e., when det(A)≠0, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with n vertices is a polygon with n vertices.

  • If T is singular, i.e., when det(A)=0, we have two additional subcases:

    • If A has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

    • If A is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with T is A=[9−33−1].

Computing the determinant of A, we obtain

det(T)=|9−33−1|=9⋅(−1)−3⋅(−3)=0.

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix.

Therefore, T is non-invertible and the image of the rectangle under the action of T is a line segment.

EXPLANATION

A square matrix A is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose: A=AT

Equivalently, aij=aji for all i,j. In other words, A is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, for any symmetric matrix A, we have (AA)T=ATAT=AA.

  • Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrices

    A=[1−110] and B=[0111].

    However, their sum is not symmetric: A+B=[1−110]+[0111]=[1021]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, for any square matrix A, we have (A+AT)T=AT+(AT)T=AT+A=A+AT.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

after.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of *any* two $n\times n$ matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
after.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(AA)^{T} & ={A}^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =AA.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrices 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

However, their sum is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any square matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

after.worked_solution:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}-{B}^{T} \\  & =A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

after.worked_solution:
The quotient rule for derivatives gives

$$
{h}^{′}(x)=\frac{{f}^{′}(x)\cdot g(x)-f(x)\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{(g(x))^{2}}.
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{h}^{′}(1)=\frac{{f}^{′}(1)\cdot g(1)-f(1)\cdot {g}^{′}(1)}{(g(1))^{2}}.
$$

From the graph above, we obtain that $f(1)=3$ and $g(1)=2.$

Additionally:

- The slope of $f(x)$ on $x\in (0,2)$ equals $1.$ So, ${f}^{′}(1)=1.$

- The slope of $g(x)$ on $x\in (0,3)$ equals $-1.$ So, ${g}^{′}(1)=-1.$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)\cdot g(1)-f(1)\cdot {g}^{′}(1)}{(g(1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2-3\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 34
after.problem:
Calculate the determinant of the matrix
$S=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We use the cofactor expansion along the first row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(S) & ={s}_{11}{C}_{11}+{s}_{12}{C}_{12}+{s}_{13}{C}_{13}+{s}_{14}{C}_{14} \\  & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2{C}_{12} \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}∗ & 2 & ∗ & ∗ \\ 1 & ∗ & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & ∗ & -5 & 4 \\ 4 & ∗ & 2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(-1)^{1+2}|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -5 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & 4 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}|-0\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|+0\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|) \\  & =-2((-5\cdot 2-4\cdot 2)-0+0) \\  & =-2\cdot (-18) \\  & =36\end{aligned}
$$

Question 36
?

Consider the matrix A=[5332]. Which of the following statements are true?

  1. a11=5 and det(A)=1
  2. xTAx is positive-definite
  3. A is positive-definite
a
II and III only
b
I and III only
c
I and II only
d
I only
e
I, II, and III
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let Δi for i=1,2,…,n denote the leading principal minors of an n×n matrix A. Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form xTAx (as well as the matrix A) is

  • positive-definite if and only if Δi>0 for all i=1,2,…,n,

  • negative-definite if and only if, for all i=1,2,…,n, we have Δi<0 when i is odd, and Δi>0 when i is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, a11=5 and det(A)=|5332|=1.

  • Statements II and III are true. Notice that Δ1=a11=5>0,Δ2=|5332|=1>0. So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form xTAx, and the matrix A, are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

- ${a}_{11}=5$ and $det(A)=1$
- ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- $A$ is positive-definite
after.worked_solution:
Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=5$ and 

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|=1.
$$

- Statements II and III are true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=5>0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}|=1>0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

after.problem: Find the curvature at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0.$
after.worked_solution:
Let $T(t)$ denote the unit tangent to the given curve as a function of the parameter t. Since we are given the curve r(t) parametrized by the parameter 
t (not the arc length s), we will use the following formula for the curvature

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ &  \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

since $t>0.$ 

Hence, the corresponding unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the curvature for  $t>0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the curvature for  $t>0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$

after.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{6} \\ y=-5\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=-\frac{y}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{6}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=-\frac{y}{5}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{5} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{6})}^{2} \\ -\frac{y}{5} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{36}) \\ -\frac{y}{5} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{18} \\ y & =-5+\frac{5{x}^{2}}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=-5+\frac{5{x}^{2}}{18}.$

We will use the formula

dydt=ddt(3t)=3

f(r(t))=(2−2t)+3(3t)=2−2t+3t.

Evaluate ${\int }_{C}(x+\sqrt{3y})\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path traversed along the line segment from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

The curve $C$ is a line segment with endpoints $(2,0)$ and $(0,3).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨(2+t(0-2)),\,(0+t(3-0))⟩ \\  & =⟨2-2t,\,3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$

Computing $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\sqrt{3y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2-2t)+\sqrt{3(3t)} \\  & =2-2t+3\sqrt{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2-2t+3\sqrt{t})\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-2t+3{t}^{1/2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{[2t-{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3[(2(1)-(1)^{2}+2(1)^{3/2})-(0)] \\  & =3(3) \\  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Express z=6−1+i in the form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ).

a
z=3(cos⁡(7π4)+isin⁡(7π4))
b
z=23(cos⁡(π4)+isin⁡(π4))
c
z=32(cos⁡(5π4)+isin⁡(5π4))
d
z=2(cos⁡(3π4)+isin⁡(3π4))
e
z=32(cos⁡(3π4)+isin⁡(3π4))
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express the given complex number in the form z=x+yi. To do this, we remove i from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of z by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is −1−i: z=6−1+i=6(−1−i)(−1+i)(−1−i)=6(−1−i)(−1)2−i2=6(−1−i)1+1=3(−1−i)=−3−3i

In polar form, r represents the magnitude |z|. For a complex number z=x+yi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=x2+y2.

So, for z=−3−3i, the magnitude is r=|z|=x2+y2=(−3)2+(−3)2=18=32.

In polar form, θ represents the argument arg⁡(z). Since x=−3 and y=−3 are both negative, z lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find θ as follows: θ=arg⁡(z)=π+arctan⁡|yx|=π+arctan⁡|−3−3|=π+arctan⁡1=π+π4=5π4

Finally, we write the complex number z in polar form: z=32(cos⁡(5π4)+isin⁡(5π4))

after.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

history.problem: Express $z=\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $-1-\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{6}{-1+\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1+\text{i})(-1-\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{(-1)^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6(-1-\text{i})}{1+1} \\  & =3(-1-\text{i}) \\  & =-3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

 

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=-3-3\text{i},$ the magnitude is 

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

    

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=-3$ and $y=-3$ are both negative, $z$ lies in the third quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-3}{-3}| \\  & =\pi +\operatorname{arctan}⁡1 \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=3\sqrt{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4}))
$$

Express z=52+4i in the form r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ). Give θ in radians to three decimal places.

a
52(cos⁡(5.176)+isin⁡(5.176))
b
25(cos⁡(4.381)+isin⁡(4.381))
c
25(cos⁡(1.107)+isin⁡(1.107))
d
45(cos⁡(3.871)+isin⁡(3.871))
e
52(cos⁡(0.381)+isin⁡(0.381))
Don't Know
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we express the given complex number in the form z=x+yi. To do this, we remove i from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of z by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is 2−4i: z=52+4i=5(2−4i)(2+4i)(2−4i)=5(2−4i)22−16i2=10−20i4+16=1020−2020i=12−i.

In polar form, r represents the magnitude |z|. For a complex number z=x+yi, the magnitude of z is given by |z|=x2+y2.

So, for z=12−i, the magnitude is r=|z|=(12)2+(−1)2=14+1=54=52.

In polar form, θ represents the argument arg⁡(z). Since x=12 is positive and y=−1 is negative, z lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find θ as follows: θ=arg⁡(z)=2π−arctan⁡|yx|=2π−arctan⁡|(−1)(12)|=2π−arctan⁡2≈5.176, rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we write the complex number z in polar form: z=52(cos⁡(5.176)+isin⁡(5.176)).

after.problem: Express $z=\frac{5}{2+4\text{i}}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give $\theta $ in radians to three decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ To do this, we remove $\text{i}$ from the denominator by multiplying the numerator and denominator of $z$ by the complex conjugate of the denominator, which is $2-4\text{i}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\frac{5}{2+4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{5(2-4\text{i})}{(2+4\text{i})(2-4\text{i})} \\  & =\frac{5(2-4\text{i})}{{2}^{2}-16{\text{i}}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10-20\text{i}}{4+16} \\  & =\frac{10}{20}-\frac{20}{20}\text{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=\frac{1}{2}-\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+1} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=\frac{1}{2}$ is positive and $y=-1$ is negative, $z$ lies in the fourth quadrant. So, we can find $\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{(-1)}{(\frac{1}{2})}| \\  & =2\pi -\operatorname{arctan}⁡2 \\  & ≈5.176,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. 

Finally, we write the complex number $z$ in polar form:

$$
z=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5.176)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5.176)).
$$

EXPLANATION

We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of e. This gives the following:

eln⁡(3x)≤eln⁡(x−1)+5eln⁡(3x)≤eln⁡(x−1)⋅e53x≤(x−1)e53x≤e5x−e5e5≤(e5−3)xx≥e5e5−3

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

3x>0⇒x>0x−1>0⇒x>1

Our solution is x≥e5e5−3, which can be expressed as [e5e5−3,∞). Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x>0 and x>1, which can be expressed as (0,∞) and (1,∞) respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

[e5e5−3,∞)∩(0,∞)∩(1,∞)=[e5e5−3,∞)

Therefore, the solution is x∈[e5e5−3,∞), which can also be written as x≥e5e5−3.
after.name: Question 44
after.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)\le \operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)+5.$
after.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} & \le {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)+5} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)} & \le {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)}\cdot {e}^{5} \\ 3x & \le (x-1){e}^{5} \\ 3x & \le {e}^{5}x-{e}^{5} \\ {e}^{5} & \le ({e}^{5}-3)x \\ x & \ge \frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >0 \\ x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x\ge \frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3},$ which can be expressed as $[\frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>0$ and $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(0,\infty )$ and $(1,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
[\frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3},\infty )\cap (0,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=[\frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in [\frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x\ge \frac{{e}^{5}}{{e}^{5}-3}.$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

x+1>0⇒x>−1x−1>0⇒x>1

Our solution is x>1+e4e4−1, which can be expressed as (1+e4e4−1,∞). Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are x>−1 and x>1, which can be expressed as (−1,∞) and (1,∞) respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

after.problem: Solve the inequality $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-4<\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1).$
after.worked_solution:
We use each side of the inequality as an exponent of $e.$ This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)-4} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)} \\ {e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}\cdot {e}^{-4} & <{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)} \\ (x+1){e}^{-4} & <x-1 \\ (x+1) & <(x-1){e}^{4} \\ x+1 & <x{e}^{4}-{e}^{4} \\ 1+{e}^{4} & <x({e}^{4}-1) \\ \frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1} & <x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we must only keep the solutions that are in the domain of the logarithms in the original inequality. To find the domain of the logarithms, we recall that the argument of the logarithm must be positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >-1 \\ x-1 & >0 & ⇒ &  & x & >1\end{aligned}
$$

Our solution is $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},$ which can be expressed as $(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ).$ Additionally, the domains of the logarithms are $x>-1$ and $x>1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1,\infty )$ and $(1,\infty )$ respectively. To find the solutions that are in the domains of the logarithms, we take the intersection:

$$
(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )\cap (-1,\infty )\cap (1,\infty )=(\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty )
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1},\infty ),$ which can also be written as $x>\frac{1+{e}^{4}}{{e}^{4}-1}.$

after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(2)Δ{x}_{1}+f(4)Δ{x}_{2}+f(8)Δ{x}_{3}+f(10)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $Δx$ | $2$ | $4$ | $2$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈5\cdot 2+3\cdot 4+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 2 \\  & =10+12+4+2 \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

a

Correct
EXPLANATION

In this case, we have n=4 rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

A≈f(1)Δx1+f(3)Δx2+f(6)Δx3+f(7)Δx4,

where each Δxi is calculated by considering the step between a particular x-value and the next one, i.e.,

Δxi=xi+1−xi.

We set up a value table that includes the Δx's.

x 1 3 6 7 9
Δx 2 3 1 2 −
f(x) 2 4 7 10 12

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get A≈2⋅2+4⋅3+7⋅1+10⋅2=4+12+7+20=43.

after.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(1)Δ{x}_{1}+f(3)Δ{x}_{2}+f(6)Δ{x}_{3}+f(7)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $1$ | $3$ | $6$ | $7$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $12$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈2\cdot 2+4\cdot 3+7\cdot 1+10\cdot 2 \\  & =4+12+7+20 \\  & =43.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Write the equation of the hyperbola $4{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2}=40$ in standard form.
after.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, to write the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to divide both sides of the equation by $40$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2} & =40 \\ \frac{4{y}^{2}}{40}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{40} & =\frac{40}{40} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The product rule for double summations states that

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{i}{b}_{j}={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{b}_{j}.
$$

\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}3{a}_{i}(4-{b}_{j}) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the rules for single summations, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}3{a}_{i}{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}(4-{b}_{j}) & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot ({\sum }_{j=1}^{12}4-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3{\sum }_{i=1}^{15}{a}_{i})\cdot (4{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}1-{\sum }_{j=1}^{12}{b}_{j}) \\  & =(3\cdot 30)\cdot (4\cdot 12-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (48-45) \\  & =(90)\cdot (3) \\  & =270\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we take the factor 3 outside the summation:

∑k=1q3Δzk=3∑k=1qΔzk

Note that ∑k=1qΔzk is just the length of the interval [1,5], because

∑k=1qΔzk=(z1−z0)+(z2−z1)+(z3−z2)+⋯+(zq−zq−1)=(z1−z0)+(z2−z1)+(z3−z2)+⋯+(zq−zq−1)=−z0+zq=zq−z0=5−1=4.

Therefore,

3∑k=1qΔzk=3⋅4=12.
after.name: Question 52
after.problem: Let $P={{z}_{0},{z}_{1},…,{z}_{q}}$ be a partition of the interval $[1,5].$ If $Δ{z}_{k}={z}_{k}-{z}_{k-1},$ calculate ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we take the factor $3$ outside the summation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}3Δ{z}_{k}=3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that ${\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}$ is just the length of the interval $[1,5],$ because

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k} & =({z}_{1}-{z}_{0})+({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})+({z}_{3}-{z}_{2})+⋯+({z}_{q}-{z}_{q-1}) \\  & =(\cancel{{z}_{1}}-{z}_{0})+(\cancel{{z}_{2}}-\cancel{{z}_{1}})+(\cancel{{z}_{3}}-\cancel{{z}_{2}})+⋯+({z}_{q}-\cancel{{z}_{q-1}}) \\  & =-{z}_{0}+{z}_{q} \\  & ={z}_{q}-{z}_{0} \\  & =5-1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
3{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}Δ{z}_{k}=3\cdot 4=12.
$$

\begin{aligned}9\cdot {6}^{x} & \ge {7}^{1-x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(9\cdot {6}^{x}) & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡({7}^{1-x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡9+\operatorname{ln}⁡({6}^{x}) & \ge (1-x)\operatorname{ln}⁡7 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡9+x\operatorname{ln}⁡6 & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡7-x\operatorname{ln}⁡7 \\ x\operatorname{ln}⁡6+x\operatorname{ln}⁡7 & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡9 \\ x(\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\operatorname{ln}⁡7) & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡9 \\ x & \ge \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡9}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\operatorname{ln}⁡7}\end{aligned}
$$
